Restaurant reservations

Diners look up restaurants, check which tables are free tonight and book one. Looking is easy to speed up. Booking is not: two people must never get the same table. Friday at 5 pm is the busy moment. Practise this easy system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

Draw your design, run a full traffic day and see how it holds.

Play this problem

The brief

Diners look up restaurants, check which tables are free tonight and book one. Looking is easy to speed up. Booking is not: two people must never get the same table. Friday at 5 pm is the busy moment.

Think of a booking site like OpenTable.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
6 million diners a month (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
6,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 1,500 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 80%; Write: 15%; Sign-in: 5%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 500 ms; Write: ≈ 500 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $2,500
Data at rest
≈ 0.3 TB
Where users are
North America: 80%; Europe: 20%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds
Fresh reads
People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • Estimate bookings from the write share at the Friday peak.
  • One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).
  • All numbers are rough approximations.

Questions that shape the design

Can the list of free times be a little old?

Yes, by a minute. If a time has just gone, the booking step says so politely.

Can the booking step be old?

No. The final check must use the real table count, so a table is never given out twice.

How many people look compared with people who book?

About 5 people look for every 1 who books (approx.).

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 17:00 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic reaches 3 times the scheduled load; rises over 30 seconds, holds for 900 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds.

  2. 12:10 · Cache stampede

    The cache empties (restart, purge, mass expiry) and every request rushes to the database at once.

    Recovery window: ≈ 300 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Looking and booking need different promises. Which can use an old copy and which cannot?
  • A longer cache time saves the database, but shows tables that are already gone. A minute is a good middle.
  • One database that serializes bookings is simple and correct. Spreading bookings over many databases needs care to keep the promise.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Which copy is the truth
  • Remembering answers

Related problems

  • Easy

    Shopping cart

    Shoppers browse products, drop things in a cart and come back later from another phone. Browsing is most of the traffic and can be a little old. The cart itself must always show what the shopper just added.

  • Medium

    Hotel booking

    You run a hotel booking site. People search for rooms, open hotel pages and book. Search can be a little behind, but you must never sell the last room twice. Bots copy your prices all day, and sometimes the payment company slows down.

  • Hard

    Airline booking

    You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day.

  • Easy

    URL shortener

    People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.
